...So what is the downside to the "diversity" agenda"? Since all change involves giving up one thing in order to embrace something else, what are we giving up?

Apparently a lot. In a large study of nearly 30,000 people across the country, Harvard political scientist Robert Putnam, author of Bowling Alone, has shown some highly negative results from "diversity."

Michael Jonas, in an article called "The Downside of Diversity," published in Boston.com in 2007, encapsulated Putnam's research as follows:

[T]he greater the diversity in a community, the fewer people vote and the less they volunteer, the less they give to charity and work on community projects. In the most diverse communities, neighbors trust one another about half as much as they do in the most homogeneous settings. The study, the largest ever on civic engagement in America, found that virtually all measures of civic health are lower in more diverse settings.

A good and enjoyable travel takes a lot of planning. Preparing for your trip can ensure you experience the most and you do so without paying yourself sick or getting into trouble. The planning phase is especially crucial when you are travelling on your own – in a vast country such as Australia. So, here are the crucial things to know when travelling alone in Australia. With these tips, you’ll be able to make the most of your journey, stay safe and have an affordable holiday.

Pack smart

When you are travelling alone, you obviously have to look after your stuff alone. So, don’t pack your bags with tons of clothing and stuff you won’t need – keep it casual and smart. Test out your backpack with all your items in it. Can you manage carrying it around for a few hours? If not, try reducing the items. It’s not too hard to find public laundry facilities in the country to ensure you can re-wash your cloths. Invest into some good travelling shoes and pack layers to stay warm, but not too hot.

Book accommodation for the first and last night in the country

If you are thinking about criss-crossing across the country, you probably won’t havea set plan on where you’re staying at any given moment. Booking accommodation while you’re in the country is not difficult and it could help you cut down costs, as you can shop around and get good value for your money. Nonetheless, since you are travelling alone, you should have a safe and secure spot to sleep in on your first two nights in the country and the final two at the end of your journey. This can reduce stress and guarantees people know where you are on those important points in your journey.

Join YHA

Speaking of accommodation, it’s a good idea to join the Youth Hostel Association (YHA) before heading out to down under. The membership card can cost less when signed up for in Europe or the US, and with the card, you can enjoy discounts on various things – from activities to hostel nights. Find out more on the website.

If hostels are not your thing, consider staying in private accommodation. Private accommodation helps you get to know the locals better. Just make sure you pick a host with a good reputation and always let someone know where you are staying.

Skip flying if you can

Australia is a giant of a country and you can’t appreciate the size until you spend some time there. But the vastness also means getting from Point A to Point B is not always easy and flying might seem like the best idea. But flying can be rather expensive and travelling by bus you often get to experience more of the country. You could even consider renting out a car and going on a road trip. Car rental companies like Hertz continuously offer discount vouchers, which can be accessed at OZCodes, and these are great for cutting the cost of driving around. The mentioned platform also has deals with Australian buss and airline companies in case you want to use these transport methods instead.

Keep people informed

Solo travelling doesn’t mean you should go incognito. For security reasons, you should keep relevant people informed of your location. This means letting your native embassy know of your travel plans and keeping your friends or family informed of your current location at all times. You could even agree certain ‘contact moments’ to guarantee authorities are alerted as soon as possible if something goes wrong.

Follow the marked trails and avoid walking around at night

Australia offers plenty of great hiking opportunities and you should definitely experience the outback as part of your journey. But don’t be heroic and go off the beaten path – it’s easy to get lost in the country and its mobile network is not reliable in the outback. You also shouldn’t walk around alone late at night, especially in remote areas, whether in the city or suburbia.

Don’t be afraid of being a ‘tourist’

Although you might like to do things on your own, you shouldn’t be afraid of doing the ‘touristy’ things. Many tours to famous places like Uluru and Kangaroo Island are affordable if booked with voucher codes and offer much more than if you experienced them on your own. Not only does it add a bit of security to your travels, tours are also great for meeting new people and finding a travel friend.

So, there are a few things you should know when travelling alone in Australia. The key is to draft a travel plan, even if you don’t mind changing it. Don’t forget to stay alert – be open-minded and don’t be too afraid, but don’t throw caution to the wind either. And when you do go out, don’t forget to share your story with Elephant Journal. The country is a fantastic location for a great adventure.
